solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Plain fool having chart reversed

indicators.note: something reversed is turned back to front, so the letters built so far are read from the end

parts.note: a sap is a gullible fool
a map is a chart

explanation.surface: Someone dim-witted holds a chart upside down while lost on a plain.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal applies to the whole fool-plus-chart string, not just to the chart, which is the trap if you try reversing MAP alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The pampas are the vast treeless grassland plains of South America, so the word names a kind of plain.

clue.text: From the first over, not the last over

indicators.note: 'not the last' tells you to drop the final letter of the word it attaches to

parts.note: over means above, in position
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator recalls every over from the very first except the final one.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'over's do different jobs: the first is a synonym trimmed of its last letter, the second the cricket abbreviation. AB OVO is Latin, literally 'from the egg'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means from the very beginning, starting at the origin of a matter, exactly 'from the first'.

clue.text: Stupid missing beer when carrying round?

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it, so one piece holds another inside it

parts.note: a pint is a glass of beer
less can mean without, as in 'a year less a day'
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A drinker feels foolish having no beer when it is their turn to buy a round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like a round of drinks in this pub picture, but it is just the letter shaped like a circle, slipped in after the first letter of the beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pointless is senseless or futile, so it can describe a stupid idea or act.

clue.text: Church trading is set up with wealth, but not European

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'set up' means raised from bottom to top, so the letters read upward

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round

indicators.note: 'but not' excludes something, telling you to take a letter away

parts.note: money is wealth
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A church's commercial dealings are established with money, excluding anyone from Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: Simony is named after Simon Magus, who tried to buy spiritual power from the apostles in Acts.
explanation.definitionFit: Simony is the buying or selling of church offices or sacred things, a form of ecclesiastical commerce.

clue.text: High water tide came twice but only going halfway

indicators.note: going only halfway means stopping at the midpoint, so the back half of each word is lost

parts.note: taken as written, then halved and doubled
taken as written, then halved and doubled

explanation.surface: A high tide came in twice but only reached halfway up the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twice' doubles each half: the first halves of the two words are each written two times.
explanation.definitionFit: Lake Titicaca on the Peru-Bolivia border is among the highest navigable lakes in the world, a body of water at great altitude.

clue.text: Tilting glass which needs to be blown

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for 'something which needs to be blown'

parts.note: transverse means lying across, sideways rather than upright
a flute is a tall narrow champagne glass

explanation.surface: A tipped glass, perhaps of a hot drink, needs blowing on to cool it.
explanation.walkthrough: The glass looks like something a glassblower makes; instead it is the champagne glass, and the blowing belongs to the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The concert flute, held sideways, is a wind instrument played by blowing across its mouthpiece.

clue.text: Branch of maths to one who explored surface elements in geometry

parts.note: taken as written
Marco Polo, the Venetian explorer

indicators.note: the surface of a thing is its outside, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: A tribute to a geometer who studied the parts of surfaces, leading to a new branch of maths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surface' is apt twice over: topology studies surfaces, and here it means the outside letters of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Topology is the mathematical study of properties of shapes preserved under continuous deformation, a recognised field within mathematics.

clue.text: Unusual Times clue for mosquito

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
X is the multiplication sign, read as 'times'

explanation.surface: A setter for The Times newspaper writes an odd clue for the insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' poses as the newspaper running this very puzzle, but it is the multiplication sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Culex is the genus of common house mosquitoes, so its name stands for a kind of the insect.

clue.text: Pest of fowl and fish

parts.note: a cock is a male domestic fowl
the roach is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: A farmer complains about a parasite that plagues both poultry and fish ponds.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a parasite that troubles poultry and fish; the two creatures simply sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: The cockroach is a scuttling household insect regarded as vermin, the classic kitchen pest.

clue.text: Singular dislike, having hit parking light

parts.note: S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular
odium is hatred or strong dislike
to lam is to thrash or hit
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A driver with a peculiar grudge has crashed into a parking light.
explanation.walkthrough: LAM, meaning to beat, is a less familiar word for hit.
explanation.definitionFit: A sodium lamp is the orange-glowing street lighting fixture, so it is a kind of light.

clue.text: Places crossed by Agricola coming west

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west is right to left, so the letters run backwards
to be crossed by something is to have it run through you, so the letters lie inside the words

parts.note: the run of letters inside the name

explanation.surface: The Roman general Agricola marched west across various places in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: Agricola was the Roman governor of Britain who campaigned westwards and north, so the surface is a history lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: Loci is the Latin plural of locus, a word meaning position or site, so it matches places.

clue.text: Courses involving home programmes

indicators.note: to involve is to include within, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: routes are courses taken
to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: Educational courses that include broadcasts you can watch at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' looks like the definition, with programmes as its partner; it is the outer piece and the definition is at the other end.
explanation.definitionFit: Routines are fixed sequences of actions or computer instructions, which is what programmes are.

clue.text: Instability and rage when females go for extravagant living

indicators.note: when something goes it leaves, so those letters are removed

parts.note: flux is a state of constant change
fury is rage
F is the abbreviation for female, one for each word

explanation.surface: Women leave a turbulent, angry life behind in exchange for a lavish lifestyle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Females' is plural because a letter goes from each of two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Luxury is a state of great comfort and lavish spending, which is what extravagant living describes.

clue.text: Duck by English river

parts.note: a duck is a score of zero in cricket
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A duck paddles beside an English river.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck in cricket is a batter's score of nothing, so it gives the word for zero.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nile in Africa is one of the world's longest waterways, an example of a river.

clue.text: Fossil I assume must keep dropping from sky

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so one piece holds another

parts.note: taken as written
guano is bird droppings
to don clothes is to put them on, to assume them

explanation.surface: Someone presumes a fossil must have fallen from the sky, like a meteorite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I assume' reads as a single thought but splits: the pronoun and then a verb meaning put on.
explanation.definitionFit: The iguanodon was a large plant-eating dinosaur known from fossil remains, one of the first ever identified.

clue.text: Record of muscular output and therefore pulse

parts.note: ergo is Latin for therefore
gram is chickpea or similar pulse, the edible seed

explanation.surface: A medical chart of muscle work and, as a result, heart rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' sits among medical words and looks like a heartbeat; here it is the edible seed, as in lentils.
explanation.definitionFit: An ergogram is the tracing produced by an ergograph, which measures the work done by muscles.

clue.text: Plant set to introduce delivery routes

indicators.note: to introduce something is to bring it in, so one piece is put inside another

parts.note: to gel is to set, as a jelly does
rounds are regular routes for delivering milk or post

explanation.surface: A factory is ready to bring in new distribution routes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like an industrial site in this business picture; it is the botanical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Groundsel is a common yellow-flowered weed of the daisy family, a type of plant.

clue.text: Safe heads needed in massacre

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
the heads are a ship's toilets; loo is British slang for toilet

explanation.surface: Protective headgear was needed during a slaughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Safe heads' reads as protected heads; instead it is a safe and a toilet, the heads being a naval word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Peterloo Massacre of 1819 in Manchester saw cavalry charge a crowd demanding parliamentary reform, killing many.

clue.text: Speculators place bets regularly in rigged surges

indicators.note: to place something in is to put it inside, so one piece goes within another
something rigged has been tampered with, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: doing something regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: Market speculators keep placing wagers on surges that have been manipulated.
explanation.walkthrough: The alternate letters are the even ones here; the odd ones would not fit the shuffled word.
explanation.definitionFit: A speculator makes risky predictions about future prices, so in a loose sense is one who guesses.

clue.text: What's round area outside of Honolulu?

definitions.text: What's round area outside of Honolulu?

parts.note: O is round in shape
A is the abbreviation for area

indicators.note: the outside of a word is its edge, so only the first and last letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: A geography question asks what land surrounds the city of Honolulu.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: Honolulu is on this island, so the island is the area all round the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Oahu is the Hawaiian island on which the state capital stands, so it is the land encircling the city.

clue.text: Moment before lighter brings about city burning during war

parts.note: a mo is a moment, as in 'half a mo'
a lighter is a flat-bottomed barge, as is a scow

explanation.surface: A cigarette lighter is flicked just before a city goes up in flames during a conflict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lighter' wants to be something that makes fire, which suits the burning city; it is a cargo barge.
explanation.definitionFit: Moscow was largely destroyed by fire in 1812 during Napoleon's invasion of Russia.

clue.text: Popular drink for prisoner?

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
mate is a South American herbal tea

explanation.surface: What is the favourite drink among people in jail?
explanation.walkthrough: MATE, pronounced mah-tay, is a caffeinated infusion drunk in Argentina and nearby countries.
explanation.definitionFit: An inmate is a person confined in an institution, most often someone held in jail.

clue.text: Freely answer Democrat politician

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer
D is the abbreviation for Democrat
Lib is short for a Liberal politician

explanation.surface: An American Democrat politician answers questions openly.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbreviations come in a row, and the politician is from the other party, not the Democrat already named.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad lib is Latin shorthand for 'at pleasure', meaning without restraint or preparation, as much as one likes.

clue.text: Showing disapproval of fine poet when cancelling book

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads

indicators.note: to cancel something is to strike it out, so a letter is removed

parts.note: Robert Browning, the Victorian poet
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: Critics disapprove of a fine poet who cancelled a book deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet loses the letter for book from his front, then the letter for fine goes before.
explanation.definitionFit: To frown is to furrow the brow in displeasure, so the participle describes a disapproving expression.

clue.text: See only a subset of men at a lot of births

indicators.note: seeing only a subset means looking at part of a run of letters, so the word lies inside them

parts.note: the run of letters straddling the words

explanation.surface: Only a few men are present at many births.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A lot of' wants to go together; split it so 'of births' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal is the adjective relating to birth, as in antenatal and postnatal care.

clue.text: One admired artificial language learner

parts.note: Ido is a constructed language derived from Esperanto
L is for learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A student of an invented language is much admired.
explanation.walkthrough: Ido, launched in 1907 as a reformed Esperanto, is a favourite crossword constructed language.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is a person greatly adored or revered, such as a pop star with devoted fans.

clue.text: UN's ethical bombing for missile installation

indicators.note: bombing blows things apart, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The United Nations approves an ethical bombing campaign against a missile base.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored; only the letters count.
explanation.definitionFit: A launch site is the facility from which rockets or missiles are fired, a military installation.

clue.text: Unfortunately none obey a single order?

definitions.note: a noun phrase for an adverb: in an order where each comes singly

indicators.note: things that turn out unfortunately go wrong, so these letters end up in a wrong order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Sadly, nobody follows even one command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a command; read as sequence, a single order is a queue of individuals.
explanation.definitionFit: One by one means individually and in succession, each person or thing taken separately in turn.

clue.text: Irresponsibly filmed orca eating director's head

indicators.note: to eat something is to take it inside, so one piece swallows another

parts.note: Willy is the killer whale in the film Free Willy

indicators.note: the head of something is its top, so only its first letter is used

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: A captive killer whale behaves recklessly by biting a film director's head.
explanation.walkthrough: Free Willy (1993) is the film about an orca, so the filmed orca is named Willy.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting wildly means behaving without restraint or care, an adverb close in sense to recklessly.
